title: On Voronoi’s Projective Model of Hyperbolic Geometry
text:
Voronoi’s Projective Cone
We begin with a question.
Let \(D=D^2\) be the two-dimensional unit disk \(D=\{z| |z| \leq 1\} \subset {\bf{R}}^2\). Can the reader readily construct continuous group actions \[(D, \partial D) \times GL({\bf{R}}^2) \to (D, \partial D)\] which satisfies the following properties:

the action is transitive on the interior;
point stabilizers are compact;
the action is elementary.

The final criteria (iii) is subjective, but important for calculations.
The reader has likely seen actions satisfying the first condition before, namely the group of “homographic mappings”, also known as Mobius transformations and their formulae. The action is conventionally presented in complex coordinates as \[{\bf{C}} \times GL({\bf{R}}^2)  \to {\bf{C}}, \quad (z, \begin{pmatrix}a & b \\ c & d \end{pmatrix}) \mapsto (az+b) / (cz+d),\] after we identify \({\bf{R}}^2 \approx \bf{C}\). But does anybody really understand the above formula? Is the formula for Mobius transformations not incredible?
JHM Labs has always found the Mobious formula \(\frac{az+b}{cz+d}\) hard to understand. Indeed we argue that it’s not elementary in the sense of (iii). Is it elementary that \({\bf{R}}^2\) possesses a division operation \((u,v)\mapsto u/v\)? Thus we argue that Mobius formulas are not elementary.
We propose the following description of an elementary action of \(GL({\bf{R}}^2)\) on the disk \(D\). The description arises from representation theory. It begins with:
(a1) The matrix group \(GL({\bf{R}}^2)\) acts on \({\bf{R}}^2\) via matrix multiplication \(\rho:(v,g) \mapsto v.g\).
(a2) The above representation has natural dual representation \(\rho^*\) of \(GL({\bf{R}}^2)\) acting on the vector space of linear functionals \({{\bf{R}}^2}^*\), where we adopt left action \(g.\ell(v):=\ell(g^{-1}(v))\).
(a3) The symmetric square of the dual representation \(Sym^2(\rho^*)\) yields \(GL({\bf{R}}^2)\) acting on the vector space of homogeneous symmetric quadratic polynomials on \({\bf{R}}^2\).
(a4) We restrict \(Sym^2(\rho^*)\) to the convex cone \(Q\) of semidefinite quadratic states which satisfy \(q(v) \geq 0\) for all \(v \in {\bf{R}}^2\). The cone \(Q\) is Voronoi’s cone of quadratic states.
(a5) The affine action \(Q  \times GL({\bf{R}}^2)\to Q\) commutes with the scalar \({\bf{R}}^{\times}_{>0}\)-action. Thus \(GL({\bf{R}}^2)\) acts continuously on the projectivization \(Proj(Q):=(Q-0) / {\bf{R}}^{\times}_{>0}\). But the projectivization of a cone is an affine bounded topological disk. Thus we find \(PGL({\bf{R}}^2)\) acts nontrivially on the bounded disk.
One finds the criteria (i), (ii), and (iii) are satisfied for every representation in steps (a1)–(a5). Thus we
Claim: The natural action of \(GL({\bf{R}}^2)\) on the projectivized Voronoi cone \(Proj(Q)\) is an elementary group action satisfying criteria (i), (ii), (iii) above.
Historically the diverse models of hyperbolic geometries discovered by Gauss, Bolyai, Lobachevskii, Beltrami, Poincare, Klein, Minkowski, etc.. are all unified with Voronoi’s projective model. Indeed we observe that all the historical models are noncanonical sections of the projectivization \(Q - 0 \to Proj(Q)\). For example, the hypersurfaces \(\{\text{tr}=1\}\) and \(\{\text{ disc }=1\}\) yield the Klein and Minkowski models of the hyperbolic plane. Compare (Thurston 2014), (Thurston 2022, 27:Ch.2). We remark that trace and dicriminant are defined as tensors on quadratic states.
This idea about Voronoi’s projective model has applications to Teichmueller spaces, and to arithmetic groups like \(Sp({\bf{R}}^{2g})\) and \(\Gamma=Sp({\bf{Z}}^{2g})\). From Voronoi we learn the idea that there can exist many “equivalent” models of a given moduli space, but they are different sections of a universal projective model.
For example, the symmetric space associated to the group \(Sp({\bf{R}}^{2g})\) is well-known as Siegel’s upper half space \({\bf{H}}_{2g}\) consisting of complex \(g \times g\) matrices \(Z\) which satisfy \(Im(Z)>0\). This latter condition implies the Gaussian \(e^-Z\) is absolutely convergent. Compare Folland’s treatment (Folland 1989).
For Teichmueller space, the existence of a universal projective model is an open problem. Geometers are not easily moved past the Teichmueller metric, which strikes us as simple an arbitrary canonical section of a projectivization not yet understood.
[To be continued - JHM]

title: On C.A. Feinstein’s Elegant Argument that P neq NP (Update)
text:
JHM Labs continues to finalize our formalization of C.A. Feinstein’s elegant argument that \(P \neq NP\). A key element in our approach is Tao-Szemeredi’s Regularity Lemma, which increasingly impresses us as a fundamental result of mathematics with wide applications to algorithms, optimal transport, and machine learning. The basic idea of Tao-Szemeredi is that correlations are deterministically determined by their marginals only so far, and beyond this determination everything is random.
We first read Craig Alan Feinstein’s paper (Feinstein 2011) in 2020. His paper was persuasive and indeed elegant, yet we understood that his argument was not completely formal and not entirely mathematical. We believe CAF’s critics are somewhat fair in their stubborn critique of CAF’s argument. Mathematicians are not artists, and they are not persuaded by impressions but require tautologies, i.e. “proofs”. Thus we took it upon ourselves to formalize and provide the mathematical foundations for his argument. This formalization is developed in our preprint (Martel 2024) available here: On C.A. Feinstein’s Elegant Argument that P neq NP.
Our approach to CAF’s elegant argument is summarized as follows:

Deciding supports of Borel-Radon measures is the Universal Decision Problem in mathematics. This is simply the measurable problem of deciding set membership, i.e. \(x\in A\).
Deterministic algorithms are exactly explicit definitions. Nothing more and nothing less.
“Guess and Check” is the Universal Deterministic Algorithm. This is admittedly difficult for mathematicians to accept, but experience and an honest review of all algorithms known to mankind to date confirms this simple observation. “How do you find a needle in a haystack? What colour am I thinking of?” The only question is whether we are performing guess and check with information, i.e. look here and not there.
Computational Complexity and Entropy are the same quantity. Essentially this means the complexity of an algorithm is measured by the memory requirements necessary to perform all the computations. I.e., log the number of elements required to support the computation.
Tao-Szemeredi Regularity Lemma (Tao 2005) implies every Deterministic Algorithm is Conditional Guess and Check (“Look here and not there”). This is the technical result underpinning our entire argument. In practice we must apply Tao-Szemeredi to the correlations basic to Zero Subset Sums.
Zero Subset Sums is a maximally unstructured decision problem according to Tao-Szemeredi Structure Lemma.
Solving Zero Subset Sums by “guess and check” over exponentially many subsets is the only deterministic algorithm to decide Zero Subset Sums, and therefore \(P \neq NP\) (Cook 2000).

These seven propositions contain the crux of C.A. Feinstein’s elegant argument.




References

Cook, Stephen. 2000. “The p Versus NP Problem.” Clay Mathematics Institute 2: 6.


Feinstein, Craig Alan. 2011. “An Elegant Argument That \(P \neq NP\).” Progress in Physics 2: 30–31.


Martel, Justin Harry. 2024. “On c.a.feinstein’s Elegant Argument That p Neq NP.” www.github.com/jhmartel/PneqNP/.


Tao, Terence. 2005. “Szemeredi’s Regularity Lemma Revisited.” arXiv Preprint Math/0504472.

title: Python Function for Minimal Energy Symmetric Operators satisfying Linear Constraints and Sylvester’s Equation
text:
We report on some progress on a technical problem which has been delaying our work.
Given arbitrary vectors \(x,y \in {\mathbf{R}}^N\), we’re looking for a python code minEnergySymmSolve to yield the minimal \(L^2\)-energy symmetric matrix \(A\) which solves the linear equation \(Ax=y\). Thus we study the optimization problem of minimizing \(||A||^2\) subject to the linear constraints \(Ax=y\) and \({}^t A = A\). We introduce the Lagrangian \[L(A, \lambda, \mu):=\frac{1}{2}{tr}({}^t A A) + {}^t \lambda \cdot (Ax-y)  ~+ \langle\mu, {}^tA -A \rangle, \] where \(\lambda\) is \(N \times 1\) vector, \(\mu\) is \(N\times N\) matrix, and \(\langle, \rangle\) is scalar-valued dot product between the \(N \times N\) matrices. Computing gradients we have \[\nabla_A L = A + \lambda \cdot {}^t x + \nabla_A \langle \mu, {}^t  A -A \rangle.\] The gradient of the third term \(\nabla_A \langle \mu, {} ^t A - A \rangle\) is computed in explicit coordinates with \(A=(a_{ij})\). We find \[\langle \mu, {}^t A -A \rangle = \sum_{ij} \mu_{ij} (a_{ij}-a_{ji}).\] To compute this gradient, we continue \[\nabla_A \langle \mu, {}^t A - A \rangle = ( \frac{\partial}{\partial a_{kl}} \sum_{ij} \mu_{ij} (a_{ij}-a_{ji}) )_{kl} = (\mu_{kl}-\mu_{lk})_{kl} = \mu - {}^t \mu.\]
Thus we find \[\nabla_A L = A + \lambda .{}^t x + \mu - {}^t \mu.\] Moreover we have \[\nabla_\lambda L = Ax -y = 0\] and \[\nabla_\mu L = {}^t A - A = 0\] according to the linear constraints.
Now some algebra. The transpose of \(\nabla_A L=0\) yields \[\lambda = ||x||^{-2} (-y + ({}^t\mu - \mu)x ) \] and \[A  = ||x||^{-2} y.{}^tx + (\mu^{t} - \mu) (Id - ||x||^{-2} x .{}^tx ).\]
Thus we find \(A\) is a function of the antisymmetric matrix \(X:= {}^t \mu - \mu\), and we look to uniquely define \(X\) rather than \(\mu\). In this notation \[A =||x||^{-2}.y.{}^t x + X.(Id -||x||^{-2}.x.{}^tx), \] and we observe that this is the general form of operators satisfying \(Ax=y\).
The symmetry constraint \({}^t A = A\) is equivalent to the following linear system, remembering that \(X\) is antisymmetric \({}^t X = -X\). We have \[{}^tA  = ||x||^{-2}x.{}^ty - (Id - ||x||^{-2}.x.{}^tx).X.\] So \({}^t A = A\) if and only if \[ ||x||^{-2} (x.{}^ty - y.{}^tx) = X.(Id - ||x||^{-2}.x.{}^t x) + (Id - ||x||^{-2}.x.{}^t x).X .\] This is a Sylvester system of the form \[BX+XB=C\] where \[B:=Id - ||x||^{-2}.x.{}^t x\] and \[C:=||x||^{-2}(x.{}^t y-y.{}^t x).\] Using SciPy solver we write X := solve_sylvester(B,B,C). Given the Sylvester solution \(X\) we obtain the matrix \(A\) according to the previous formula \[A =||x||^{-2}y.{}^t x + X.(Id- ||x||^{-2} x.{}^t x).\] It’s important to verify that \(A\) is indeed symmetric and numerically solves the linear system \(Ax=y\).

import numpy as np
from scipy.linalg import solve_sylvester

# xarg is 1xN np.array
# yarg is 1xN np.array
# returns the minimal energy symmetric NxN matrix A which maps Ax=y

def minEnergySymmSolve(xarg,yarg):
    x = xarg.T
    y = yarg.T
    n = len(xarg[0])
#    print("n",n)
    id = np.eye(n)

    scalar1 = ((x.T)@x)[0][0]  #np.dot(x.T,x)[0][0]  # tx.x = |x|^2 sum of squares
    scalar2 = scalar1**-1  # inverse square |x|^{-2}

    matrix1 = x@(x.T)  # x.tx
    matrix2 = np.dot(scalar2,matrix1)  # |x|^{-2} x.tx
    B = np.subtract(id, matrix2)  # B = Id - |x|^{-2} x.tx ... symmetric 
#    print("B symmetric", B)
#    print("B eigenspectrum \n", np.linalg.eig(B))  # print the eigenspectral data
    matrix3 = y@x.T  # y.tx
    matrix4 = x@y.T  # x .ty
    C = np.dot( scalar2 ,matrix4 - matrix3) # C = |x|^{-2}(x.ty - y.tx) ... antisymmetric
#    print("C antisymmetric", C)
    
    # Solve for X
    X = solve_sylvester(B, B, C)  # X is the solution of XB+BX=C ... necessarily antisymmetric.  
#    print("Verifying Sylvester Solution:", )
#    print("X antisymmetric", X)  # Verify X is antisymmetric.

#    print("X@B", X@B) # X @ B = X @ (Id - |x|^{-2} x.tx)
#    print("B@x=0?", B@x)  # this quantity needs to be zero!
    matrix5 = np.dot(scalar2, y@(x.T))  # |x|^{-2} y.tx 
    A = matrix5 + (X @ B)  # A = |x|^{-2} y.tx + X (Id - |x|^{-2} x.tx)
#    print("A", A)
    
    return A

We report on some progress on a technical problem which has been delaying our work.
Given arbitrary vectors \(x,y \in {\mathbf{R}}^N\), we’re looking for a python code minEnergySymmSolve to yield the minimal \(L^2\)-energy symmetric matrix \(A\) which solves the linear equation \(Ax=y\). Thus we study the optimization problem of minimizing \(||A||^2\) subject to the linear constraints \(Ax=y\) and \({}^t A = A\). We introduce the Lagrangian \[L(A, \lambda, \mu):=\frac{1}{2}{tr}({}^t A A) + {}^t \lambda \cdot (Ax-y)  ~+ \langle\mu, {}^tA -A \rangle, \] where \(\lambda\) is \(N \times 1\) vector, \(\mu\) is \(N\times N\) matrix, and \(\langle, \rangle\) is scalar-valued dot product between the \(N \times N\) matrices. Computing gradients we have \[\nabla_A L = A + \lambda \cdot {}^t x + \nabla_A \langle \mu, {}^t  A -A \rangle.\] The gradient of the third term \(\nabla_A \langle \mu, {} ^t A - A \rangle\) is computed in explicit coordinates with \(A=(a_{ij})\). We find \[\langle \mu, {}^t A -A \rangle = \sum_{ij} \mu_{ij} (a_{ij}-a_{ji}).\] To compute this gradient, we continue \[\nabla_A \langle \mu, {}^t A - A \rangle = ( \frac{\partial}{\partial a_{kl}} \sum_{ij} \mu_{ij} (a_{ij}-a_{ji}) )_{kl} = (\mu_{kl}-\mu_{lk})_{kl} = \mu - {}^t \mu.\]
Thus we find \[\nabla_A L = A + \lambda .{}^t x + \mu - {}^t \mu.\] Moreover we have \[\nabla_\lambda L = Ax -y = 0\] and \[\nabla_\mu L = {}^t A - A = 0\] according to the linear constraints.
Now some algebra. The transpose of \(\nabla_A L=0\) yields \[\lambda = ||x||^{-2} (-y + ({}^t\mu - \mu)x ) \] and \[A  = ||x||^{-2} y.{}^tx + (\mu^{t} - \mu) (Id - ||x||^{-2} x .{}^tx ).\]
Thus we find \(A\) is a function of the antisymmetric matrix \(X:= {}^t \mu - \mu\), and we look to uniquely define \(X\) rather than \(\mu\). In this notation \[A =||x||^{-2}.y.{}^t x + X.(Id -||x||^{-2}.x.{}^tx), \] and we observe that this is the general form of operators satisfying \(Ax=y\).
The symmetry constraint \({}^t A = A\) is equivalent to the following linear system, remembering that \(X\) is antisymmetric \({}^t X = -X\). We have \[{}^tA  = ||x||^{-2}x.{}^ty - (Id - ||x||^{-2}.x.{}^tx).X.\] So \({}^t A = A\) if and only if \[ ||x||^{-2} (x.{}^ty - y.{}^tx) = X.(Id - ||x||^{-2}.x.{}^t x) + (Id - ||x||^{-2}.x.{}^t x).X .\] This is a Sylvester system of the form \[BX+XB=C\] where \[B:=Id - ||x||^{-2}.x.{}^t x\] and \[C:=||x||^{-2}(x.{}^t y-y.{}^t x).\] Using SciPy solver we write X := solve_sylvester(B,B,C). Given the Sylvester solution \(X\) we obtain the matrix \(A\) according to the previous formula \[A =||x||^{-2}y.{}^t x + X.(Id- ||x||^{-2} x.{}^t x).\] It’s important to verify that \(A\) is indeed symmetric and numerically solves the linear system \(Ax=y\).

title: Weber, Clausius, Entropy, and Thermodynamics
text:
The classical reference for entropy is Clausius 1865 (Clausius 1865), which introduces the term \(S\) as “the entropy of a body, from the Greek word ‘τροπή’ (transformation), because in the processes of nature this quantity always changes in a definite direction.”
Clausius further states “The energy of the universe is constant. The entropy of the universe tends to a maximum.” This contains the principle of the First Law of Thermodynamics, and Clausius’ Second Law of Thermodynamics. .


In Gibbs’ book (Gibbs 1902) we find the problem of deriving the First Law of Thermodynamics from mechanics, namely \[ dU = TdS - \sum F dx\] where \(W=\sum Fdx\) represents work on the mechanical system, and \(dU\) represents the change of internal potential energy of the system. Many references describe the First Law as represented by \(dU = T dS - PdV\) where \(PdV\) represents pressure across the change in volume. This latter term is equivalent to the work performed by the pressure along the boundary of the volume. Note pressure is defined only along the boundary of the volume in the above expression.
We derive the First Law of Thermodynamics from Weberian mechanics as follows.
First recall the primary equation of classical mechanics, namely Newton’s \(F=F_{local}=ma\), which we rewrite as \(F_{local}-ma=0\). This latter step is simple and important. It suggests replacing \(F_{local}\) the sum of all forces acting on \(x\) with the sum of all forces acting on \(x\) in the universe \(F=F_{local}+F_{nonlocal}\). Thus we replace \(F_{local}-ma=0\) with the equation of dynamic equilibrium \[\sum F=0.\]
This balance of forces becomes the primary law of mechanics. It includes the equations of Newtonian mechanics by explaining the mass acceleration term \(-ma\) as equal to the nonlocal force \(F\) exerted by the universe at infinity on \(x\). We experience inertial masses as constant because the universe at infinity is basically constant on average in our reference frame. The sky at infinity does not move that much relative to our frame. This is a form of Mach’s principle that inertial mass is defined by our motion relative to the stars at infinity (Mach 1883). See Halton Arp’s lecture on intrinsic red shift.
The Principle of Dynamic Equilibrium can equivalently be expressed as the Principle of Zero Energy \(\sum U = 0\). We emphasize that this expression represents the sum of all local and nonlocal interaction energies. This means energy is conserved globally at all times, but locally varies according to \(\Delta U_{local} = -\Delta U_{nonlocal}\). Stability of nonlocal interaction potential yields the usual Conservation of Energy of closed systems. Therefore energy can be created and destroyed locally, but the sum over all interactions is zero. “The only constant is everything adds up to zero.”



The Weberian perspective on thermodynamics is that energy strictly manifests in two forms: potential \(U\) and kinetic \(T\). Weber defines potential as the potential for productive work, i.e. the potential for matter to be put in linear parallel motion having kinetic energy. Here “work” means applying a force to an object in a linear motion, i.e. apply a force through a distance. Thus work consists of matter being put into relative motion.
The distinction belonging to the First Law of Thermodynamics is that matter in motion, can be decomposed into “Random” plus “NonRandom” motion. The Random motion is incoherent and does not add to any large scale bulk linear motion. The parallel part of the kinetic energy is that part of the motion which results in productive work. The random incoherent part is the entropy expression represented by the term “\(T.dS\)” as we propose below.
The internal potential energy of a system is extracted by the environment into work, but this work is not necessarily coherent nor productive. That part of the work which is unproductive is represented by the entropy term and repesents random KE. This represents the Clausius kinetic view on entropy and temperature.
The thermodynamic definition of Temperature is according to the formula \[T=\frac{\partial U}{\partial S}\] of the two extensive variables \(U, S\) of potential energy and entropy, respectively. There is interesting remark in [BBC, In Our Time, Science, Episode on Heat] which gives the Scottish Glaswegian definition of entropy as representing the loss of available work, or in our terms, the loss of available productive work in a system. Thus entropy represents that part of the kinetic energy which is random and adds up incoherently to zero, and represents that part of kinetic energy which does not contribute to the productive work performed by the system.
The thermodynamic variables \(U,S\) are extensive with respect to a system \(X\) in the sense that they are \(1\)-homogeneous with respect to the state variables. The ratio \(T = dU/dS\) implies \(T\) is an intensive variable (\(0\)-homogeneous with respect to state variables) designating “temperature” (and not kinetic energy per the usual notation). This amounts to the Zeroth Law of Thermodynamics. But it still begs the question “how to represent the random kinetic energy?”
Remark. The 19th and 20th century had a broader heterogeneous view of energy and energy radiation, e.g. photon radiation, gravitational radiation, electromagnetic, etc.. The Weber perspective, by contrast, follows Ampere’s original idea that primary laws of physics need be homogeneous. Thus Weber explains all forms of energy transfer as various expressions of a homogeneous system of energy transfer, namely between potential and kinetic energy according to Weber electrodynamics.



Water flows.
Water flows wherever it has the opportunity to flow.
Water will flow whenever it can flow.
Water never forfeits the opportunity to flow.
This is like electrical discharges. All the potential at high voltage exists, but it does not discharge without a conducting path, without an opportunity. Moreover it immediately discharges if there is a conducting path.
This surprises us sometimes. It accounts for the particular direction of time in our opinion. We remind the reader that we take the Machian perspective of time as “matter in motion” (Mach 1883).
Where did we first learn of this idea? We can’t recall…
The principle of minimal internal potential energy expresses the idea that any system \(X\) in an environment \(E\) will have all its available capacity for work extracted by the environment. We are reminded of a scene at UofT, an old Soviet era professor saying, “Well, if there was any object [X], then it’s gone they stole it.” Once we know the environment has a positive need and demand for work, then it’s clear that any available potential energy will be extracted by the environment. This is why the hot cup of coffee becomes cold. It’s subject to the environment. We are always competing with the environment, which looks to seize upon all available potential and translate this energy into incoherent kinetic energies which have no bulk state of motion. If one leaves potential energy subject to the environment, it is almost certainly gone when we come back.
To belabour the point yet further, consider the basic so-called law of supply and demand. The law includes the proposition that wherever there is supply, and wherever there is demand, there is also the transfer of the goods. This represents our basic idea about the Principle of Minimal Potential Energy. It is a property of the external environment. The internal potential energy is only minimized to the extent that the environment can absorb this potential and translate it into kinetic energy (either random or coherent).
Basic thermodynamics states that entropy \(S\) is defined as the Fenchel-Legendre transform \(S=U^*\) of the potential energy. Therefore the entropy \(S\) is maximized wherever the potential energy is minimized according to the constraints. Compare (Cullen 1969).
A similar idea is that minimum potential energy is equivalent to maximal environmental extraction of work. If a system has the potential to do productive work, and the environment has a need for productive energy, then the environment will extract the energy and convert into KE. This is the idea that water flows and will flow. Therefore states with some initial potential energy will have this potential converted into kinetic energy at the first environmental opportunity. A state always reduces to a ground state, relative to the environment, after the environment has extracted the maximal amount of productive work from the system’s potential.
Test Question: Why does temperature \(T\) flow from hot to cold? Why is there strictly monotone flow of thermal energy? What can we predict about the asypmptotic temperature distributions in closed systems, can we predict the homogenization? The equilibration of temperatures in a closed system is equivalent to sayng the random kinetic energies of all particles eventually become equidistributed, i.e. they all become equally random in magnitude. [insert proof]
Idea: KE is expansive and interactive. KE seems very good at distributing and equilibriating. [c.f. Equipartition of Energy].
Clausius Statement: “Heat cannot spontaneously flow from a colder body to a hotter body without external work being done.”
How is this interpreted by Weber? We have two bodies \(B_1\) and \(B_2\), say \(B_2\) is the environment. Suppose that the random KE of \(B_1\) is less than the random KE of \(B_2\). Then Clausius says there is a definite transfer of KE from \(B_2\) to \(B_1\) in the absence of any external work. Contrapositively, there is no transfer of heat (random KE) from \(B_1\) to \(B_2\) without external work.



The Shannon information entropy is basically \(\log(\text{number of states})\). If a physical system has high entropy, then there is alot of random KE and the positions and velocities of any particles cannot be known with any certainty. On average the magnitude of the velocities might be known, but the direction and position of these particles will not be known. The information about the position and velocities has alot of random variation, as determined by the random KE, and this corresponds to information uncertainty.

title: Weber, Mendeleev, Periodic Table of Elements (Briefly)
text:
Bounded Orbits and \(\{H<0\}\)
In this post we want to describe a simple idea. Consider the Weber Hamiltonian \(H = [formula]\). Consider an initial state \(p\) which evolves according to the Weber-Hamilton equations. Then how can we predict or decide whether the orbit is bounded asymptotically as \(t\to +\infty\)?
We begin with the observation that: an orbit is unbounded if some radial distance \(r_{ij}\) diverges with \(t \to +\infty\). But this implies the Weber potential \(U_{ij}\) vanishes as \(t\to +\infty\). Conservation of Energy implies \(H=T+U\) is constant, and therefore \(H=T+0=T \geq 0\), since \(T\geq 0\) as a sum of squares.
This implies the following simple criterion: If the Hamiltonian energy is negative $ H < 0 $, then the state orbit is asymptotically bounded.
Given that negative energy states correspond to bounded states, it’s interesting to consider the problem of displacement (translation) between two negative states \(p_0\), \(p_1\). The natural question arises: Is it possible to translate \(p_t\) satisfying \(H(p_t)<<0\) for \(0 \leq t \leq 1\)? This is effectively a form of alchemy.
As we understand it, all molecules and matter consists of electrodynamics and electrons and protons. The mass difference \(m_p =1836 \times m_e\) is unexplained. Atoms are bounded electrodynamic systems. Therefore atoms correspond to negative Hamiltonian states.
What is the difference between lead and gold?
In state space we are looking to reconfigure from lead to gold. The inner atomic configurations are probably extremely different from the gold configuration. How much \([-2]\) molecules are involved in gold rather than lead? These molecules do not form of themselves, but require \(E=\mu c^2\) Joules of work from the environment.
Remark. The general problem is estimating the energy difference between two different states. How much external energy is required to reassemble the electrical systems?
Speculation. Can we assume that a state is equidistributed along the Hamiltonian energy level, i.e. does the WH-equations of motion translate initial states uniformly throughout \(H=\text{constant}\)?
